Abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.
items.author: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Ying Xu, Siyuan Zhang

items.title: Patch-Based Deep Kernel Learning for Data Assimilation and Bias Correction with Extremely Sparse Observations
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41596v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data Assimilation (DA) reconstructs the state of a spatio-temporal system by combining sensor observations with the output of a numerical model. Since model states are high-dimensional while observations cover only a small fraction of the domain, DA is a challenging large-scale estimation problem, central to weather forecasting and oceanography. Classical variational methods such as 3D-Var rely on a hand-crafted background error covariance that assumes unbiased errors, and therefore cannot capture state-dependent correlations or systematic model biases. Moreover, their cost grows with the size of the domain. Deep learning (DL) methods can perform DA and bias correction (BC) non-linearly, but typically offer limited interpretability and no calibrated uncertainty estimates. We propose a hybrid framework that couples a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a learnable-kernel Gaussian Process (GP) to jointly perform DA and BC from extremely sparse observations. The model is trained end-to-end by maximizing the marginal log-likelihood, learns a data-driven covariance over the whole grid, and provides both the Maximum A Posteriori analysis and its uncertainty by design. A patch-based strategy reduces the $O(N^3)$ training cost of exact GPs over $N$ grid points to $O(N)$ for a fixed patch size. Inference remains exact and only requires solving a linear system whose $O(m^3)$ cost depends on the number of observations $m \ll N$, not on the domain. The learned covariance can also replace the hand-crafted one in 3D-Var, improving its accuracy without changing the variational formulation. Experiments on sea surface temperature and salinity, with both synthetic and real, extremely sparse in-situ observations, show that the framework outperforms 3D-Var, a classical GP and a competing DL model, while reducing inference time by more than 98% with respect to 3D-Var.
items.author: Emanuele Mele, Angelo Coluccia, Massimo Cafaro, Italo Epicoco, Paola Nassisi

items.title: Connectivity-Aware Client Selection in Decentralized Federated Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) has emerged as a scalable alternative to centralized federated learning, removing the single point of failure and communication bottleneck at the server. However, most existing decentralized approaches rely on full-neighborhood broadcasting, where each client transmits its model update to all of its neighbors in each communication round. While effective, this results in significant communication overhead and high energy consumption. This paper applies spectral graph tools as lightweight client selection methods that leverage the graph topology by analyzing the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian over a fixed communication graph. Specifically, we exploit eigenvector embeddings and heat/diffusion kernel similarities to guide each client in selecting only a subset of structurally relevant neighbors, i.e., those that are most beneficial for the convergence of the federation process. This topology aware randomization matches or outperforms uniform neighborhood subsampling and approaches the accuracy of full broadcasting. The largest gains, about $3$ percentage points, emerge under strong data heterogeneity on larger, structurally rich graphs, while the total number of transmitted messages is reduced by $50\%$ compared to naive broadcasting.
items.author: Usevalad Milasheuski, Monica Nicoli, Stefano Savazzi

items.title: Verify--Backtrack Loop: Structured Precondition Recovery for Long-Horizon Language Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, where actions often depend on latent preconditions. The core difficulty is not trajectory length but recovery: when a prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition fails, trying another plausible action rarely helps. ReAct and later reflection or adaptive-planning methods support local correction, but express recovery as free-form text, with no explicit control state linking the terminal goal, the active goal, and the failure source. We introduce the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL), a training-free extension of ReAct that turns precondition discovery and failure diagnosis into structured planning-state updates. VBL maintains the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack and, on goal activation, execution failure, or material state change, jointly verifies two horizons---whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state. These dual-horizon judgments, combined with typed failure attribution, trigger explicit operations---Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo the parent. We evaluate VBL with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld. VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone--benchmark pair. On the challenging AppWorld setting, it improves task success by up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct. Ablations show that removing either verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct, confirming that the two mechanisms are complementary. These results show that reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state, not merely the next action.
items.author: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan, Xin Li, Linqi Song

items.title: Specification-Guided Generation for Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41511v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.
items.author: Alessandro Previti, Konstantinos Vandikas, Mario Alviano, Mats Carlsson, Albin Larsson Forsberg, Alexandros Nikou, Athanasios Karapantelakis, Aneta Vulgarakis

items.title: Multi-Test Nation Bias Benchmarking of LLMs with Explicit Unbiased Baselines
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41486v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While prior work has highlighted that systematic nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) can pose operational risks for international relations (IR) applications, many existing evaluations still lack a clearly specified unbiased reference (ground truth), limiting fully quantitative and cross-setting measurement. Using an expanded corpus of 722 official UN Security Council (UNSC) records, we measure nation-level bias with five complementary tests, thereby extending prior approaches to cover a broader set of bias expression channels: opinion ranking (WOW), association sorting (AK+-), vote simulation (PVS), opposition attribution (F-Oppose), and framing (Headliner). To enable grounded bias evaluation, we explicitly define an unbiased status for each test; in particular, for WOW and AK+- where ground truth is difficult to specify, we propose an action-based pseudo unbiased status derived from observable voting behavior to construct a quantifiable baseline. Benchmarking 4 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral-22B-Small, and Qwen3-30B) across the five permanent members of the UNSC, we find a test-agnostic macro-pattern: relative to the reference baselines defined for each test, model outputs lean toward the opposition (red) side for China and Russia and toward the supportive (blue) side for the U.K., the U.S., and France. These results underscore the need to audit IR-facing LLM deployments with grounded, multi-test benchmarks tied to explicit reference points.
items.author: Jonghyeon Choi, Yeonjun Choi, Beakcheol Jang

items.title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41479v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/xagao/EvoMCP.
items.author: Xuanang Gao, Kepeng Lin, Xinyan Shi, Yong Deng, Shuheng Shen, Changhua Meng, Xiaofeng Wu, Jie Yang, Wei Liu

items.title: Evidence-Guided Recovery for AI Agents with Ambiguous Tool Outcomes and Partial Execution
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41453v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool timeouts can leave AI agents facing ambiguous tool outcomes and partial execution: an action may have failed, committed or remained in flight while other workflow steps have already completed. We formulate evidence-guided task recovery over approved obligations, provider capabilities and states compatible with public evidence. A shared admissibility check handles key expiry, authorization timing, dependencies and residual effects; a terminal certificate separates actual goal satisfaction from publicly supported safe completion. The known-model implementation combines standard observation-contingent planning with a separately implemented effect-history adjudicator. In a finite study of 37 assignments, planning and three active controls each certify 28 completions; four saved synthetic fee units incur additional computation. A preregistered assignment-held-out comparison then evaluates planning advice against evidence prompting with two local model bundles. Across 58 paired units in 19 previously developed task families, advice certifies 30 completions versus 9, a 36.2-percentage-point difference (exact family sign-flip p=0.0078), using 272 proposals versus 399. All 116 trajectories pass independent replay. Both models exhibit a positive completion difference. The comparison measures the evaluated advice interface under a common shield; search-versus-rule advice requires a separate matched comparison. Unknown and handoff outcomes remain explicit, with guarantees tied to the declared provider capabilities rather than arbitrary third-party exactly-once execution.
items.author: Genliang Zhu, Xiaobo Chen, Ziyuan Wang, Chu Wang

items.title: CryoAtlas: A Large Curated Dataset and Unified Benchmark for Cryo-EM Atomic Model Building
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep learning has accelerated automated atomic model building from cryo-EM maps, yet progress remains limited by the lack of large, high-quality datasets and standardized evaluation benchmarks. We address this gap by introducing CryoAtlas, a rigorously curated dataset and unified benchmark for density-guided atomic model building of protein chains. By integrating and filtering EMDB and PDB entries (up to March 2026), CryoAtlas provides 17,809 map-model-sequence entries, including a curated 16,657-entry training split. From this resource, we construct a 618-target benchmark with a shared evaluation protocol that jointly assesses structural accuracy, model-to-map fit, and stereochemical validity. Using this framework, we benchmark state-of-the-art learning-based methods against Phenix and AlphaFold3, comprehensively analyzing the impact of map resolution, sequence length, protein category and sequence identity on modeling accuracy. As a case study, retraining the ModelAngelo CNN component on CryoAtlas improves performance on the benchmark. CryoAtlas provides an open, reproducible foundation for future cryo-EM atomic model building research. Project details and resource release updates are available at https://oulling.github.io/cryoatlas/.
items.author: Mingrui Li, Minzhang Li, Weichen Qin, Yufan Xie, Zhangzhi Xiong, Sixian Shen, Jiakai Zhang, Yuan Pei, Jingyi Yu

items.title: scAnyOmics: Foundation-Model Distillation for Any-to-Any Completion of Multi-omics Virtual Cells
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41399v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in single-cell technologies have enabled the profiling of multiple molecular modalities, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and chromatin accessibility, providing a more comprehensive understanding of cellular states. However, integrating heterogeneous modalities and predicting missing molecular information remain challenging, particularly when paired measurements are limited. Here, we introduce scAnyOmics, a generative framework that distills knowledge from a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student model. scAnyOmics integrates scRNA-seq, protein-marker measurements, and scATAC-seq into a shared representation, enabling cross-modal prediction and reconstruction of missing modalities. We assembled 690,880 cells from six publicly available studies, covering both paired and partially paired multi-omics measurements, to systematically evaluate its predictive performance. We further evaluated scAnyOmics on held-out donor data, where it outperformed baseline methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Beyond cross-modal reconstruction, we explored its applications in cell-type annotation, perturbation-response prediction, and biological age estimation. Overall, scAnyOmics provides a unified framework for integrating incomplete single-cell multi-omics data and transferring pretrained biological knowledge, supporting the development of virtual cell models across diverse cellular contexts and experimental platforms.
items.author: Zhaoqi Song, Ye Du, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo, Qian Niu

items.title: Cross-Interface Authorization for AI Computer-Use Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computer-use agents act through graphical interfaces, command lines, APIs, scripts, and Model Context Protocol servers. A policy decision can be interface-invariant while its executable authorization is not: another route can bypass mediation, alter a security-relevant default, or commit after the authorized state has changed. We present a profile-bounded protocol for a fixed, versioned computer-use deployment. It enumerates effect-bearing routes and durable sinks, checks a route-to-sink enforcement cut, normalizes each concrete request to a canonical effect, issues a route-bound prepare ticket, and verifies the route, effect, grant, trace, profile, inventory, and authoritative state again at commit. A committed result requires an agreeing sink receipt. Under explicit assumptions, we prove profile-bounded refinement, matched-effect decision invariance, resistance to alternate-route laundering and declared cross-surface recomposition, commit-time state safety, and receipt-grounded outcomes.
  The reference profile registers 12 effect families, five interfaces, and 60 routes. Two structurally distinct runtime mappings produce 3,464 traces over 1,732 scenarios each: 960 commits, 2,312 denials, and 192 commits after re-preparation. An independent checker accepts every retained trace and pair and rejects 26/26 semantic regressions; coverage and normalizer suites reject 24/24 and 720/720 mutants; and 168/168 commit probes match their declared outcomes. A frozen-source audit passes 52 checks over 12 files from two independent hybrid runtimes and one public authorization substrate. Source-shaped adapter refinements commit 48/48 instrumented calls and reject 15/15 unbound cases. The resulting guarantees bind the declared profile and its effect semantics.
items.author: Genliang Zhu, Chu Wang

items.title: Online Evidence-Containment Prediction over Text Spans under Distinct Queries
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41384v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evidence-grounded NLP systems often verify nested text regions sequentially, so verifying one region constrains others. We formalize this as Online Evidence-Containment Prediction (OECP): each candidate is predicted before exact verification and queried at most once. Span containment is exactly a triangular 2D product order, making OECP distinct-query online isotonic regression. With multiple admissible targets, worst-case regret is near-linear, $\widetilde{\Theta}(m_{\mathrm{eff}})$, in the effective scale given by endpoint-rank compression; a single fixed target, as in standard QA, admits an explicit polynomial-time learner with optimal $\Theta(\log m_{\mathrm{eff}})$ regret, run on real NQ episodes. On Natural Questions, containment yields a large deductive gain plus a smaller learned gain on unresolved candidates, reproduced across two backbones and DPR hierarchies. Expected Search-space Reduction (ESR) turns these probabilities into decisions, localizing evidence in fewer verifier calls on SciFact, ERASER, and DPR hierarchies; on DPR hierarchies under call budgets it outperforms four recent external selectors and raises fixed-reader F1 over learned and generator-greedy scheduling.
items.author: Xiang Liu, Haochen Ding

items.title: Ask on Demand: Targeted Peer Communication for Parallel Agentic Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41378v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parallel LLM agents tackle complex tasks by exploring multiple trajectories, yet useful discoveries remain isolated in individual execution histories. Existing sharing methods often select or summarize information before other agents' needs become clear, potentially overlooking details that become important later. We propose Ask on Demand (AOD), a communication framework that enables agents to seek targeted peer assistance when specific information needs arise. Upon an approved request, AOD retrieves relevant evidence from peer execution histories, selects a suitable peer, and generates a response tailored to the request. To determine when such assistance is worthwhile, we train a lightweight gate using paired team continuations, with supervision derived from final team outcomes and inference cost. Experiments on AppWorld and WebShop demonstrate that AOD consistently improves task performance over independent parallel execution while achieving lower inference cost than existing information-sharing baselines. These findings highlight the benefits of aligning peer communication with agents' evolving information needs to achieve more effective and efficient collaboration.
items.author: Haofu Yang, Hongyang Yin, Ran Bi, Faguo Wu, Peng Xue, Feng Zhou, Han Zhang

items.title: From the Zoo to the BULLPEN: Sample-Efficient LLM Profiling via Multi-Channel Model Embeddings
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41375v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Choosing among the hundreds of thousands of available large language models (LLMs) requires a thorough understanding of each candidate model's properties. In practice, each property is measured by its own benchmark suite, so profiling a model on many properties means paying for many separate evaluations. To address this, model embeddings compress each model into a fixed-length vector from which many properties can be predicted. Existing methods, such as EmbedLLM, build these vectors from correctness patterns and question features, and often need large probe batteries to do so. However, many behaviors that are important when choosing a model, such as its verbosity, safety and style, show up more in how it answers than in whether it is correct. We introduce BULLPEN (Behavioral Understanding of Large Language models via Profile ENcodings), a framework that extends EmbedLLM in three ways. First, BULLPEN organizes the downstream tasks that prior work uses and adds 20 task benchmarks we built on behavior, style and provenance. Second, it is the first framework to read a model's own answer text jointly with its correctness and the question text. Third, it encodes models from a few hundred questions instead of the full 24,118-question pool. Across 260 open-weight models, our answer-text encoder scores 0.48 +/- 0.10 on the new tasks against 0.35 +/- 0.10 for the best prior encoder. Our encoders that read answer text keep at least 91% of their full-pool skill from only 400 questions (1.3% of the inference compute of the full question pool), while a correctness-only baseline keeps 83% with the same 400 questions. Because these embeddings need only model outputs, they support behavioral auditing and low-cost profiling, and could extend to API-only models. Code and data: https://github.com/wcquesera/bullpen
items.author: Russell Ro, Qiming Cui, Reza Abbasi-Asl

items.title: RECITE: Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Overly restrictive eligibility criteria contribute to widespread enrollment failure in clinical trials, yet published recommendations for how specific criteria should be broadened remain disconnected from trial design at scale. We introduce RECITE (Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence), a framework for automated discovery, extraction, and implementation of evidence-based eligibility criteria revisions. RECITE uses protocol amendment documents from ClinicalTrials.gov to construct a dataset of 11,913 curated instances across 5,735 trials, each pairing original criteria with documentary evidence and target revisions. We benchmark fifteen LLM configurations under truncated-to-context-window and retrieval-augmented generation conditions, on a 3,116-instance sample under an LLM-as-judge protocol validated against ten domain experts (judge vs. human quadratic-weighted Cohen's $\kappa_{qw} = 0.694 \pm 0.096$). The best open-weight model, Gemma 2 9B, achieves $\kappa_{qw}$-aligned ordinal score $3.0 \pm 0.9$ on a 0--4 scale (normalized 0.742) and the best closed-weight model, GPT-4o, reaches $3.0 \pm 0.8$ (normalized 0.745). Using an agentic literature discovery system, we then identified 44 paper--trial matches across five publications providing trial-design and EC-modification evidence. Our findings suggest that existing clinical knowledge can be operationalized into actionable trial design recommendations.
items.author: Russell Ro, Reza Abbasi-Asl

items.title: LEAP: Efficient LLM Inference Scheduling with Generalizable Length Prediction
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41359v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.
items.author: Kwan Yan, Jialun Zhong, Yanzeng Li

items.title: Do Transaction Prices Reflect Visual Preference? A Diagnostic Study with Multimodal Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41358v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing visual preference evaluation relies on costly human annotations or preference reward models, whereas online marketplace transaction prices are readily available and reflect real purchasing behavior, offering potential low-cost supervision. However, transaction prices conflate visual preferences with non-visual factors such as provenance, demand, and competition, making aggregate accuracy insufficient to distinguish model errors, unreliable price signals, and protocol confounds. To address this identifiability challenge, we introduce MarketImage, a diagnostic framework that identifies when transaction prices reflect visual preferences, where they fail, and whether multimodal language models can recover human-supported visual preference signals. MarketImage comprises three components: (i) MarketImageArt, 266 six-image comparison sets with transaction prices and price-blind human rankings; (ii) MarketImageLens, a tie-preserving protocol that partitions 3,990 within-set image pairs into price-human agreement, conflict, and price-tie regions while separately auditing presentation-order effects; and (iii) MarketValuator, six elicitation methods spanning direct comparison, independent scoring, budget constraints, and multi-agent aggregation to evaluate signal recovery by static visual scorers and three multimodal language models. Experiments show that only 24.2% of image pairs have a non-tied price direction, of which 34.7% agree with the human majority. Within this region, HPSv2 leads at 66.4% Recoverable Accuracy; Qwen's budgeted and aggregated variants trail baselines, while GPT interface gains remain statistically unresolved. Thus, transaction prices encode recoverable visual preferences only under limited conditions and should be treated as uncertain proxies rather than ground truth.
items.author: Fengxian Ji, Jingpu Yang, Fan Zhang, Junhong Liang, Qian Jiang, Yuke Li, Jinri Guo, Rongxin Zhu, Zhuohan Xie

items.title: Operon-S1: a fast decision controller for long-horizon biomedical agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41350v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language-model agents now carry out long scientific work in biology, but their judgements about conventions, skills, errors, evidence and stopping are made inside the reasoning that does the work, where they cannot be measured, replaced or improved on their own. Here we present Operon-S1, a fast decision system, a System 1 for the agent, that separates judging from doing. A decision harness poses the agent's recurring judgements as closed questions at 13 decision points and acts only through fixed messages that never contain an answer, so any model that answers the questions can serve as the judge. Across seven life-science benchmarks, a local decision model took over these judgements in 0.6 s at the median for an in-loop request on CPU at no request cost, with no measurable change in the agent's score on five of six benchmarks, whereas the general language model that drives the agent, asked the same questions, accounted for 8.0% to 35.2% of task cost. Every decision is recorded with its consequence. Retraining on labels from task construction, verifiers or execution raised decision accuracy on every question in each of three trained versions, and a new version enters service only through a promotion gate. Task-level results in this study use the public checkpoint. The same closed decisions serve wet-laboratory protocol troubleshooting and the design of a germline target enrichment panel. Like the regulator of an operon, which switches genes on and off without making their products, Operon-S1 steers the agent without doing its work, and makes the agent's judgements a layer that can be measured, replaced and trained.
items.author: Genoria AI Team, Yuejie Hou, Yueyuxiao Yang, Weiting Tang, Meng Yang

items.title: SERIAL-7: Deriving, Realizing, and Preserving Machine-Verifiable Outputs Across Representations
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.41308v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs consumed by programs and downstream systems, where semantic correctness alone does not guarantee reliable execution. We introduce SERIAL-7, a Korean-English benchmark built around an executable verification framework for machine-verifiable generation across seven representations. Using 177 validated canonical artifacts, SERIAL-7 separates semantic derivation (Derive), constrained artifact generation (Realize), and cross-representation preservation (Preserve). Its 43 atomic representation constraints are paired with executable checks over format, structure, and task-specific semantics, enabling progressively stricter verification from representation compliance to full artifact validity. Across ten models, REALIZE-L3 HSR ranges from 42.0% to 93.9%, while Full Compliance exposes additional artifact-level failures beyond correct final answers and valid representations. These results show that reliable structured generation requires explicit, executable verification of how artifacts are realized and preserved across representations.

items.title: v2.1.316
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK, which turns the ultrathink keyword off
  • Added pooled group budgets to the Claude apps gateway: one monthly budget that a group's members share, on top of each member's own limit, set with pooled_budget on the spend limits admin API
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_LOOPED_CROSS_CERT_DROP to keep system cross-certificates that certify each other in a loop, for servers whose private CA needs one
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT to set the effort level subagents run at when nothing else names one, instead of inheriting the session's
  • Added managed.policy_mode: layered to the Claude apps gateway: every policy that matches a developer applies, each merged over the ones listed below it, not only the first
  • Added guardrail.input_tagging on Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, which wraps prompts in the input tags that an Amazon Bedrock guardrail's prompt attacks filter needs; all_messages_and_system also tags the system prompt
  • Deprecated fast mode for Opus 4.8 as of October 30, 2026; it will be removed on November 30, 2026. After removal, fast mode requests on Opus 4.8 return an error and do not fall back to standard Opus 4.8. Migrate to Opus 5.5 to keep the speedup
  • Fixed shell commands being left running on macOS and Linux when Claude Code exits by itself, for example when credentials are refused or a cloud session is archived
  • Fixed bash aliases with line breaks in their value (except in Git Bash), and functions whose names start with a dash, being garbled or lost in the Bash tool's shell
  • Fixed bash scripts started from the Bash tool stopping after their first command when SHELLOPTS is exported
  • Fixed PowerShell hooks not blocking on exit code 2 when the command begins with a type cast, param, using or an attribute
  • Fixed some network requests hanging when a compressed response was cut off or corrupted
  • Fixed sonnet, opus and haiku on Vertex AI and Amazon Bedrock showing an error mid-session instead of switching to an older model when the newest is not yet available to the account or region
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway not checking every model a request names against availableModels, deniedModels and models; a request that names a blocked model now gets a 400 naming the field
  • Fixed claude auth login refusing to run where managed settings require a Claude apps gateway; in a terminal it now shows the gateway sign-in
  • Fixed --restricted sessions uploading files from outside the working directories when a Read allow rule covered them
  • Fixed prompts containing invisible characters needing a second Enter to send; plain prompts now send cleaned on the first Enter, and commands still wait for review
  • Fixed sub-agents that inherited a parent sub-agent's model moving to the main model when a background job or message woke them
  • Fixed a managed autoMode.allow list without "$defaults" getting the built-in exceptions back from a host app's --settings, a first rule added in /permissions, or /auto-mode-setup
  • Fixed cloud sessions and cloud scheduled tasks not being marked as failed when auto mode stopped a turn because the server returned no safety verdict
  • Fixed claude -p text output sometimes not saying why auto mode stopped a turn when a background agent was still running
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 being ignored in sessions started by a host application (such as Claude Desktop) behind a proxy or LLM gateway with experimental betas turned off
  • Fixed plugin MCP headersHelper scripts receiving a corrupted CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT and server URL when a credential-named environment variable was set to a switch value such as 1
  • Fixed the SDK register_repo_root control request not loading the CLAUDE.md of a directory outside the working directory (with CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1)
  • Fixed the Artifact tool showing ? for artifact database access rules at the self level, and not quoting those rules back when it refuses a republish that would drop them
  • Fixed /model <id> not warning when the model isn't recognized by this version and auto-compact will assume a 200K context window
  • Fixed the "hold space to speak" hint using up its three showings in one session, and showing an empty key when push-to-talk is unbound
  • Fixed Grep and Glob never returning when the search process is killed at the timeout but does not exit, seen on Windows
  • Fixed a rare case where resuming a conversation did not restore its plan, when /clear or /resume had been run while part of that conversation was still being saved
  • Fixed first-run setup dropping words from the security notes and the terminal-setup explanation in narrow terminals
  • Fixed the Enterprise survey card taking a typed 1 or 0 after a short pause; a typed answer now needs Enter
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a message sent while Claude was working being answered after a Stop, once the session's process had been replaced
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server's on/off switch sometimes being lost when a session moved to a new machine
  • Windows: Fixed the Bash tool losing your aliases and functions in Git Bash when the rc file sets errexit and pipefail and only winpty aliases, or none, are defined
  • Improved /code-review started from the Code tab in Claude Desktop or on the web: cloud and claude remote-control sessions now show the findings card, not a plain-text list
  • Improved /diff on large repositories: each refresh usually runs one fewer full-repository git command, and refreshes are spaced out when git is slow
  • Improved the messages shown when /ultrareview, a cloud session or a cloud agent finds no GitHub remote: they now say to create a repository at https://github.com/new, and /ultrareview no longer suggests a gh command that gh rejects
  • Improved SSL certificate errors to name the likely causes, among them a server that leaves out an intermediate certificate, and the fix for each
  • Changed auto mode so that an autoMode.allow list without "$defaults" no longer removes the built-in rule on scheduled-task prompts
  • Changed server-managed settings for Team and Enterprise logins: settings fetched from Anthropic's API now apply without an approval prompt, and a stored copy that doesn't verify is refused
  • [VSCode] Added sign-in to a Claude apps gateway from the chat panel, with no terminal needed
  • [VSCode] Changed ultrathink to run its turn at xhigh effort and show in a rainbow in the chat box, as in the terminal
  • [VSCode] Fixed the missing Effort slider, Ultracode switch and model name when the model setting has the [1m] tag, such as opus[1m]
  • [VSCode] Fixed saved /btw side-question history being deleted too early while a settings file has errors
  • [VSCode] Fixed a conversation coming back in Auto mode after a reload or restart when its plan was approved with "Yes, and manually approve edits"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a form card to cloud sessions, so you can fill in or decline a form an MCP server asks for instead of the request being canceled without you seeing it
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a "Catching up…" line that shows while a cloud or Remote Control session you switch back to is still bringing its messages up to date
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed network secrets so Enterprise members can add and delete them on their own cloud environments, instead of only viewing them
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the Changes pane for cloud sessions: the note about what the list leaves out is now a badge beside the branch name, not a row above the diff
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed file search in a cloud session's Files pane showing folders as ../.. paths after Claude changed directory; results now show their path from the project's root
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude refusing to edit or append to a canvas it made in a Slack channel, from that channel, once the canvas was also shared to another channel or a DM
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed untagged replies going unanswered in a Slack Connect thread when both organizations have installed Claude and Slack delivered the reply to the other organization's app
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a cloud scheduled task's live status checklist in Slack staying half-done; a run can now edit the top-level messages it posted during that run
  • [Claude Tag] Changed a Slack channel's Respond automatically switch to a "How Claude participates" choice on the channel's Configure page and in Claude Tag admin settings
  • [Code Review] Added a findings-by-severity card to the Code Review analytics page, showing the period's total findings, a daily chart stacked by severity, and each severity's count

items.title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
items.summary: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents […]
items.content:
While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens.

Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI.

Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on.

The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies.

“As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.”

Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight

Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold.

At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI, a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther, a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS.

Nexus, a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument.

Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours.

Science Fact, Not Fiction

The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula. 

Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon.

Learn more about NVIDIA AI for science.

items.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
items.summary:
Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.

The post From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
At a glance

  • Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.
  • To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings.
  • The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss.
  • Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material.

Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly.

Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence.

They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in.

We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform, which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars:

  • Synthetic enterprise environments: simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data
  • Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets
  • Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation

Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data?

In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot.

Synthetic enterprise environments

Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve.

Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments: simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful.

Grounding in real world signals

To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources.

  • O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates.
  • Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions.
  • SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization.

Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure.

Industry specific simulation

We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage:

  • A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings
  • A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews
  • An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination

This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes.

Automated query generation

While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in.

The six-stage pipeline

We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios.

Validating synthetic quality

Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions:

  • Structural fidelity: Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships?
  • Contextual relevance: Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns?
  • Behavioral realism: Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics?
  • Content safety: Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals?

End-to-end automation

While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including:

  • Reproducibility: Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases.
  • Scale: The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand.
  • Iteration speed: Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles.
  • Cross-team consistency: Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels.

This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results.

PODCAST SERIES

The Shape of Things to Come

Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future.

Listen now
Opens in a new tab

Privacy and safety by design

Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline. Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk.

Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline.

This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible.

Results and impact

Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions.

On synthetic data quality, our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments.

On scale and efficiency, each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs.

On organizational adoption, our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure.

Conclusion

As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety.

Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next.

At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale.

Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets!

Opens in a new tab

The post From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence appeared first on Microsoft Research.

items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories: Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode
  • Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too
  • Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text
  • Added idle compaction to VS Code and Claude Desktop's Code tab: a 200K+ token conversation left idle is summarized, and the summary is used on your next message if the prompt cache has expired
  • Fixed sessions failing turn after turn with "Invalid effort level" when an organization's admin caps a model's effort: Claude Code now lowers the effort, retries, and says which level it uses
  • Fixed claude -p exiting with code 0 and no output when startup failed; it now prints the error and exits 1
  • Fixed Bedrock sessions with many images failing every turn and /compact with "400 Input is too long." instead of removing older images and compacting
  • Fixed Microsoft Foundry sessions failing when the resource has no deployment for the default Sonnet, Opus or Haiku model: Claude Code now falls back to an older model of that family
  • Fixed repeated refused requests behind a gateway that doesn't accept tool search's tool_reference blocks: the request is sent again once without tool search, and the session remembers
  • Fixed TLS connections failing with UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT when the system certificate store holds a renewed root certificate that is cross-signed with its predecessor
  • Fixed MCP servers that also work without sign-in showing "needs authentication" after their stored sign-in stopped working; they are now used signed out
  • Fixed claude mcp logout reporting success when the MCP sign-in was not removed, for example while the macOS keychain is locked over SSH
  • Fixed extra sign-in renewals when several sessions share an Anthropic profile login and the credentials lock is busy
  • Fixed claude ultrareview and claude remote-control asking the workspace trust question in a CI job that has a terminal; with CI set they now refuse an untrusted folder at once
  • Fixed an administrator's TLS trust settings in managed settings not being applied in Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed model switching being refused on machines with managed plugin settings when one of your own --plugin-dir or --plugin-url plugins had a broken manifest or failed to download
  • Fixed the Bedrock and Vertex model upgrade offer coming back at every start when managed settings pin the model
  • Fixed forceRemoteSettingsRefresh set only in remote managed settings no longer applying once the stored copy had expired, which let sessions start without policy when the server could not be reached
  • Fixed "Continue automatically at usage limit" continuing more than three times without a prompt from you when a task restarted itself between waits (a /goal check-in, a background or scheduled task)
  • Fixed background and cloud sessions started with Ultracode turning it back on at their next start after it had been switched off
  • Fixed the last broken reply and its retry prompts staying in the conversation after Claude gave up on a tool call that could not be parsed
  • Fixed a PreCompact hook with very large output making compaction fail or repeat; each hook's output is now cut at 10,000 characters
  • Fixed background diff refreshes briefly taking the repository's index lock, which could make a git command run at the same moment fail with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists"
  • Fixed markdown tables jumping between grid and stacked layouts on half-typed rows while streaming, and long tables falling back to raw pipes
  • Fixed the /resume picker showing the text of CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md as a session's title when the session only ran slash commands
  • Fixed /btw answering from the main conversation when asked from a subagent's open transcript
  • Fixed pasting an image over SSH to a Linux machine doing nothing silently; the prompt now says to copy the file over and paste its path
  • Fixed claude remote-control sessions that failed to start when the session service was slow for a moment: the worker's registration is now retried with growing waits
  • Fixed model switches over Remote Control that take over 8 seconds getting a "still pending" error instead of the final result
  • Fixed the sandbox.excludedCommands setting description saying listed commands always run outside the sandbox; it now says every command in a call must match an entry
  • Fixed shell and MCP calls that auto mode, a deny rule or a PreToolUse hook blocked, or that otherwise did not run, reading as if they ran in a collapsed tool group
  • Fixed sandbox protections not applying to a worktree entered by claude -p --resume or --continue
  • Fixed hooks matching Bash not running on shell commands started by the Monitor tool; such hooks can block or ask, but not approve or rewrite those commands
  • Fixed a settings file excluded with --setting-sources still supplying some settings, such as auto mode rules and saved permission consents
  • Fixed auto mode reporting a call as blocked, and listing it in /permissions, when its safety check gave no verdict
  • Fixed a Claude apps gateway Vertex upstream hanging for minutes when a Google token endpoint accepts the connection and never answers
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway's start-up warning for a deprecated Claude Desktop key that it still serves as written saying "stops being accepted" after the key's end date
  • Fixed /upgrade opening the browser and starting a new login for plans billed through the App Store or Google Play; it now says where to change the plan
  • Fixed --resume, and rewinding past a switch to another model after a refusal, moving a session on a model name Claude Code doesn't recognize to a different model
  • Fixed requests failing when a gateway or cloud provider refuses one of Claude Code's beta headers by name: the request is sent again without it
  • Fixed model IDs spelled with a dot behind an LLM gateway, such as claude-opus-4.8, being treated as an older model with the wrong context window, output limit, effort, thinking mode and cost
  • Fixed Remote Control clients showing a stray "Compacted (ctrl+o to see full summary)" row after /compact
  • Fixed the cloud sessions tip and the Remote Control idle notice showing when an organization's policy turns those features off
  • Fixed a resumed claude.ai cloud session making a model call nobody asked for when the previous worker stopped just after receiving a new chat's files
  • Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions silently dropping a PDF's text past 100,000 characters; it now says how much was unread and where to read on
  • Fixed Claude being told only that a command was declined after you stopped it with Esc or Stop in a cloud session or the IDE; it now also hears that the command may have run
  • Fixed blank lines at the top of a code block disappearing when the code block opens a quote
  • Fixed a blank line appearing above some ⎿ rows in the transcript view (Ctrl+O)
  • Fixed vim mode dw, dW, yw and yW carrying on past the end of the line, and made w and W stop on empty lines
  • Fixed x and Enter in the agent panel sometimes acting on the wrong agent when another agent started or finished
  • Fixed pasted text and dragged-in files being lost in Claude's question dialog unless the "Other" row had focus
  • Fixed pasted text being lost when a row in the prompt footer was selected
  • Fixed vim mode p over a character selection ignoring whether the yanked text was whole lines
  • Fixed vim mode aw and iw taking the line break at the end of a line
  • Fixed ↓ selecting footer items hidden by the ? help menu, the command list or a paste hint
  • Fixed Esc on a command's panel, such as /btw, also interrupting the subagent whose transcript is open
  • Fixed the welcome header in fullscreen mode showing the session's model while viewing a subagent or teammate that runs on a different model

items.title: Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #97
items.summary:
Host Sowbhagya Suresh shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from understanding the challenges facing coding agents to uncovering how people use AI at work and improving extended-range weather forecasting.

The post Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #97 appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
What’s new in research? 

You may already be familiar with the Research Focus newsletter (opens in new tab) on LinkedIn. Now, you can catch up on highlights from across the research community at Microsoft on our social channels, YouTube, and major podcast platforms, too. 

In this edition of Microsoft Research Focus, host Sowbhagya Suresh shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from understanding the challenges facing coding agents to uncovering how people use AI at work and improving extended-range weather forecasting. 

Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next.

Related links:

  • Research Focus newsletter on LinkedIn (opens in new tab)
  • ForkPilot: Self-Evolving Policy for Retrospective Search in Long-Horizon Agents
  • Code Understanding is a Bottleneck for Coding Agents
  • TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills from Offline Telemetry
  • Why Copilot use looks so similar across industries, and what that misses (opens in new tab)
  • Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
  • New AI framework bridges a critical gap in mid-range weather forecasts
  • BioEmu2 in public preview (opens in new tab)

Chapters

00:48: A self-improving agentic framework (opens in new tab)

01:35: Understanding coding agent success and failure  (opens in new tab)

02:29: Evolving agent skills with activity logs  (opens in new tab)

03:22: Looking beyond similarities in AI use  (opens in new tab)

04:15: Helping teachers make more time for teaching  (opens in new tab)

04:52: Improving extended-range weather forecasting  (opens in new tab)

05:42: BioEmu2 now available in public preview  (opens in new tab)

06:32: Final thoughts (opens in new tab)

Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:

  • Apple Podcasts
  • Email
  • Android
  • Spotify
  • RSS Feed

Transcript

[MUSIC]

SOWBHAGYA SURESH: Hi, I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Welcome to Microsoft Research Focus.

You’ve probably read our newsletter. And now you can get highlights from across the research community at Microsoft here, on YouTube, and major podcast platforms. Whether you read, watch, or listen to it, Research Focus is your source for research news at Microsoft.

Coming up in this edition: what everyday AI use reveals about the way we work; how a new AI model could help scientists better understand proteins; a new approach to improving weather forecasts weeks in advance; and more. So here’s what’s new.

A self-improving agentic framework

More and more, AI agents are handling tasks that are complex.

[MUSIC FADES]

Tasks that require multiple steps, decisions, and interactions with external tools. But how can we count on AI agents to do the work if their ability to adjust when things go wrong may require a lot of resources with no guarantees of a better result?

A new self-improving framework called ForkPilot learns when it’s worth revisiting earlier decisions to find a different approach and adapts its strategy based on new outcomes.

Tested across six benchmarks and leading AI models, ForkPilot measures up to the best existing methods while reducing AI processing demands by up to 59%. These results suggest that AI agents can solve complex problems more reliably and efficiently, making them more practical and cost-effective to deploy at scale.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Understanding coding agent success and failure

Coding agents execute user queries by reasoning about, editing, and running code. Understanding why these agents fail is critical if we want to build more capable and reliable coding agents. Unfortunately, existing benchmarks often make it difficult to identify which factors contribute to success or failure.

CABRA is a framework for generating coding challenges from scratch. It lets researchers increase complexity in a controlled way and pinpoints the skills that are most difficult for agents.

Across thousands of generated challenges, the researchers found that agents often overcame coding problems by using tools. Yet the agents still struggled when they needed to understand unfamiliar codebases. The findings suggest that understanding existing code, rather than modifying it, remains one of the biggest obstacles to developing more effective coding agents.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Evolving agent skills with activity logs

Computer-use agents are AI systems that are designed to complete tasks that require clicking and typing. They can fill in forms, process requests, and navigate websites. To do this effectively, they need to learn the procedures that people use to get work done. User activity logs can offer a way to capture this knowledge. But activity logs typically don’t record the intent behind each action and often combine tasks.

The new framework TeleTune learns reusable skills and workflows from these logs. It also infers the task goals associated with the sequences of actions.

In evaluations across software and browser tasks, TeleTune outperformed existing approaches. By learning from existing activity, TeleTune offers a scalable way to help AI agents adapt to unfamiliar software and carry out complex, multi-step workflows

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Looking beyond similarities in AI use (opens in new tab)

Workers across industries may appear to be using AI in surprisingly similar ways, but a closer look reveals a different story.

Microsoft researchers analyzed aggregated Copilot Chat activity across a broad range of customer categories and found that editing documents led all classified activities, accounting for more than 20 percent.

But when researchers set aside the 20 most common activities, differences between customer categories became substantially more pronounced. The most common uses of AI may be hiding important differences in how organizations use it for more specialized work.

For business leaders, the takeaway is clear: don’t assume you have the same AI needs as others in your industry. Finding the right opportunities means looking beyond usage statistics to understand what employees actually do, how they work, and what outcomes matter most.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Helping teachers make more time for teaching

A new study shows how Shiksha Copilot—a human-in-the-loop AI tool—could transform teacher workflows in Global South classrooms.

The study in low-resource schools in India found the tool reduced the time teachers spent on bilingual lesson planning and bureaucracy. That gave them more time to craft more engaging classroom activities.

More than a thousand teachers participated, and many reported reduced stress levels and a positive impression of how AI can help them. These teachers actively engaged with Shiksha Copilot, using their professional expertise to adapt and repurpose materials to suit their own classrooms.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Improving extended-range weather forecasting 

Ten-day weather forecasts have become remarkably dependable. But what about the weeks that follow?

The two-to-six-week window remains a major challenge for forecasting models, which is a problem. That’s when a wide range of critical decisions get made related to farming, managing wildfires, and preparing for extreme weather.

A new machine-learning framework called Probabilistic Bias Correction, or PBC, is helping close that gap. PBC learns from a weather model’s past mistakes and helps correct them.

And the early results are promising.

PBC took top honors in a global competition focused on improving extended-range forecasting. It’s also being deployed in Kenya, where it’s helping improve critical monsoon forecasts for farmers.

This development could help make weather predictions more useful across a broad range of applications.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

BioEmu2 now available in public preview (opens in new tab)

BioEmu2, a new foundation model for understanding biomolecular structure, dynamics, and function, is now available in public preview.

Developed by the Microsoft Research AI for Science team, BioEmu2 builds on Biomolecular Emulator, a deep-learning model designed to help scientists better understand how proteins work.

That understanding could have important implications for medicine. By learning more about how proteins function, scientists could move closer to developing more effective medications that enhance beneficial protein activity or prevent proteins from causing harm.

Go to the BioEmu2 Microsoft Research GitHub repository (opens in new tab) to explore the model and learn more.

From more capable AI agents to better weather forecasting, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring at Microsoft.
