items.title: How We Built Our Design Agent
items.summary:
• Taste comes from context. Models already write good code, but they need your designers’ principles, guardrails against AI slop, and the reasoning behind feedback to make work that looks like yours.
  • Give the agent a designer’s computer. Every Slack thread gets its own sandbox where the agent keeps the project between turns, works across a video engine, image tools, and a shared canvas, and inspects its own renders.
  • Delete rules when the model improves. Rules that make up for a model’s weaknesses expire, so keep the design principles and remove the workarounds as models get better.
  • Long-running agents need multiplayer UX. Big jobs run for hours on async subagents, so the Slack thread shows the plan, live progress, and an approval before anything ships, and anyone on the team can steer the agent mid-run.
  • You can fork it. The open-source repo has the full harness, and Managed Deep Agents deploys it to your team’s Slack.

‍

The promo above was made by Content Studio, our design agent that can create videos, social graphics, recreated UI images, slide decks, and more from just a single prompt in Slack. Every asset the agent produces is written in code.

Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents. It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great.

So how did we go from such low quality to this?

We've spent four months teaching Content Studio our taste and design principles, mostly by watching it get things wrong in front of the whole company.

This post walks through how our GTM Engineering team worked with our design team to build Content Studio from scratch: what good design means to us, how we taught the agent our taste, and the harness that lets it make anything from a still to a launch film.

We've open-sourced our design agent. Fork the open-source repo, add your brand tokens, fonts and skills, and deploy it to your team's Slack with Managed Deep Agents.

Then join us at GTM Engineering Live on October 28. We'll go under the hood of the harness and the UX, and show the work that didn't fit in this post.

Building a design agent for scale

LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. Our design team was stretched thin, with repetitive requests crowding out more strategic and innovative work. As a lean startup, we needed a low-friction way for anyone at the company to create high-quality, on-brand work.

To address these needs, we built Content Studio, a design agent that lives in Slack. A team member describes what they want and attaches accompanying content or briefs, and the agent returns finished, on-brand files. To build Content Studio, we needed three things:

  1. Our designers' expert judgment, written into the agent's skills and checks so it knows what good looks like.
  2. A custom environment around the model, including a video editing computer with tools for every layer of the design work.
  3. The right UX, so a whole team can collaborate on a project that runs for hours from one Slack thread.

Managed Deep Agents gave us everything we needed to productionize Content Studio inside our company: a managed LangSmith Sandbox, integration with Slack, managed tools, scoped agent memory and scheduling agent runs. This allows a small team to spend its time on the design work, the skills, tools and Slack experience, instead of the plumbing.

Key results

  • Content Studio has delivered over 3,000 assets across the company, including more than 80 slide decks. One of its decks was even used in our most-watched organic YouTube video.
  • Posts with its work drew about 4.5M views on X.
  • On the LangChain account, posts with its visuals have earned about 2x the likes and 3.7x the bookmarks of other posts.
  • Three in four requests now come from outside marketing, and 75% of users are repeat visitors who come back every week.
  • The median request now costs about 50 cents in model spend, down from about $8 in mid-September. Our own code shrank by about 80% after the migration to Managed Deep Agents.

Is AI actually good at design?

Before jumping into the build, let’s first address the debate of the century: can AI actually produce good design?

The model was already good at execution and could write HTML and CSS, chart specs and animation timelines. However, it didn't have our context, so it reached for familiar patterns, what Anthropic calls “distributional convergence”. The result could look polished and still look like a hundred others, or be beautifully animated and never get its point across. Familiar isn’t always bad, but we wanted our agent to make choices that followed its purpose.

Katie Dill, Head of Design at Stripe, makes a helpful comparison. Under pressure to build quickly after World War II, builders copied the clean shapes and bare surfaces of modernism over and over. The copies kept the look while losing the thought and character behind it. Her warning is that AI can do the same to software. She calls it “zombie UI” and says we need a point of view, because “if you don’t, AI will give it for you.”

We don't think AI is bad at design. It just doesn't have a point of view unless you provide it, and giving it ours meant teaching it our taste.

Teaching a design agent taste

Taste is the judgment that separates work that's correct from work that's good. In design, two layouts can use the right fonts, colors and spacing, and only one of them makes its point. Taste comes from what Dill calls "getting really good at noticing."

That noticing is how we learned to spot AI slop, which most often shows up when a brief leaves a decision to the agent.

For example, the image on the left below was created by a local coding agent with our brand skill (which includes colors, fonts, logos, etc.). But the final result missed critical components, such as the correct logo lockup, text alignment, and which colors were our primary vs. secondary brand colors.

The same prompt produced a perfectly on-brand image in Content Studio. This happened because the local agent filled in each decision that the brief didn't cover with what it had seen most. With this methodology, Content Studio filled the same gaps with our choices.

The guidelines we gave Content Studio started with the basics, including color tokens, font weights, spacing, and alignment. But much of the improvement came from what we added on top. We introduced design principles, like having one focal point per frame, guardrails against common AI design patterns, and the reasoning behind each piece of feedback. Combined with better underlying models, these helped Content Studio learn to think and communicate more like a designer.

It didn't start that way. In one of our early motion graphics, a bird flies off screen with a ribbon of light trailing behind it for less than a second. We asked for no sharp edges, but the first pass came back clunky, with harsh, rounded edges. A designer would have understood what we meant. The edges should soften, while the tail tapers and fades in the direction opposite the bird's movement.

By a later iteration, the agent was evaluating that detail with a designer's eye. Using a quick sketch to identify where the bird's tail should be, it built its own frame-by-frame check to ensure the ribbon stayed attached. Most viewers would never notice the detail consciously, but they'd feel it if something was off.

The measurable problems were the easiest to solve. Default capitalization used to come up frequently in reviews, but an automated check now catches every instance. The harder decisions are more subjective, like whether a campaign idea is strong enough, the message comes through clearly, or the execution resonates with the audience. When a designer makes one of those calls, we capture the reasoning in a skill so the agent can apply it to future drafts.

Content Studio changed who can do design work. A PM, engineer, or founder can brief the agent in Slack and walk away with something on brand and ready to ship. Three in four requests now come from outside marketing. For designers, the role has shifted closer to that of a creative director, setting the direction and reviewing the work rather than producing every asset themselves.

Getting the design judgment right was one part of the process. We also needed to give the agent the tools and environment to execute on it.

Building a media harness

A designer works across several tools, from Photoshop for stills and a video engine for motion to a shared canvas for prototyping and collaboration. They also rely on brand guidelines, design assets, and company documentation.

An agent needs a similar setup, with a computer to work on, tools for different parts of the design process, and the context a designer brings to their work. The harness brings these pieces together. Deep Agents provides the underlying harness, including the agent loop, planning, files, subagents, and context management. Managed Deep Agents packages and runs it in production. We built the environment around it, giving the agent a computer where it can maintain a project, work across tools, and inspect the results.

harness_v1

Our first version of that harness tried to do the designing for the model. The early models needed a lot of help to make a motion graphic or a launch film we'd want to ship. To compensate for what they couldn't yet figure out themselves, our intuition was to put more of our own design judgment into instructions and code.

So, we built a design system with 115 reusable UI components for titles, layouts, and animations, along with guidance on when and how to use them. This gave the model a set of existing designs to work from, reducing the number of creative decisions it had to make from scratch.

That helped it stay on brand, but the agent would just repeat the same layouts and animations for each frame without much variety:

We knew the models would eventually be great at this task, so we kept building the environment for that moment, experimenting with the skills and tooling along the way. Sometimes we'd add more references or more detailed instructions to help the model. Other times we'd remove them entirely and see what it could do on its own.

But the results still weren't where we wanted them, and closing the gap required increasingly more engineering work. We kept adding rules to the skills, writing more motion code, and building more components to compensate for what the model couldn't do.

Then Opus 5.5 arrived, and we saw an immediate jump in quality. We revisited the skills and removed most of the hard-coded rules, keeping the design principles and high-level guidance. The results improved further, with more variety and less repetition. The model was finally making creative decisions we'd previously tried to prebuild for it.

This was our Bitter Lesson. Rules designed to compensate for a model's weaknesses become less useful as models improve. What lasts is the environment around the model, including the tools it uses, the context it draws from, and how people guide its work. Instead of prebuilding creative decisions, we focused on making the harness flexible enough to take advantage of each new generation of models.

Designer’s computer

To show the harness in action, we asked Content Studio to make a film about how it works with a video project end to end. The result stars a parrot in a pixel jungle narrated in the style of David Attenborough (voiced with ElevenLabs). Let's use it to walk through the layers of the harness: computer, tools and context behind its work.

Design is iterative. You make something, look at it and change it, often many times. So the agent needs a computer it can keep working on across a whole conversation. Each Slack thread gets its own LangSmith Sandbox, an isolated Linux machine with a filesystem and a shell, and the project lives there for the life of the thread.

Everything the agent creates is built with code, whether it's an HTML page for a slide, a data spec for a chart, or an animation timeline for a video. This makes it easy to iterate without starting over. If someone asks to bring the parrot in earlier, the agent can change a single timing value and render again without affecting the artwork or copy. With a flat image or generated video clip, even a small edit could mean recreating the entire asset.

The brief, plan, scene code, audio and renders all live in one project folder, which every subagent on the job works from.

On top of that, we installed the tools a designer would reach for at each layer of the work:

Motion is the most difficult layer. It runs on two engines:

  1. HyperFrames for editing: HyperFrames, HeyGen's open-source video framework, turns a video into a web page. Clips, screen recordings, captions and text are just elements on that page, and a GSAP timeline moves them around. So when someone asks to caption a webinar or cut a product demo, the agent edits it like a web page. Its CLI is basically the agent's editing suite: lint the composition, pull a frame to check, render the cut. We also install HeyGen's official skills, so the agent learns the format from the people who built it.
  2. motion-studio for animation: A web page can't blur fast motion, make things glow or turn a logo in 3D, and that's the finish we wanted for original animation. So we built our own canvas engine. The agent writes code that draws every pixel of every frame, and the engine blends up to 16 moments into each one, the same way a camera shutter blurs movement. The parrot film was made this way.

Both engines render each frame based on its timestamp, so a frame at ten seconds looks the same regardless of when it's rendered. This lets the agent inspect individual moments without rendering the entire film, while also allowing us to render multiple frames in parallel. Audio runs on the same timeline, keeping narration, music, and sound effects synchronized with the visuals.

With this setup, the agent can create almost anything. But without further guidance, it defaults to the model's own design choices rather than ours. The next challenge was teaching it to work within our brand and design standards.

Designer's brain

We organized the agent's knowledge around four distinct functions, each with a clear purpose. Skills guide how to perform specific tasks, while the wiki provides context about our company and what good work looks like. Anything measurable is handled by a gate, a deterministic check written in code. A separate memory layer captures what people teach the agent over time.

Skills

The first thing the agent does with a request is work out what kind of job it is. That's handled by our media-production skill. We call it a router skill because most of it is one table. Each row maps a kind of ask (a campaign, a restyle, a thumbnail, a post, a YouTube package, a launch film, a short animation) to the path and the specialist skill that handle it. The router also decides whether the work needs a shared visual canvas, and it keeps small edits out of the full process.

For a film like the one above, the router picks the launch-film skill designed for directing a large motion production. Each of our 48 skills, close to 1,000 files in all, is scoped to a job rather than a topic, so its description reads like a routing rule, including when not to use it.

Skills compose instead of repeating each other. launch-film directs and motion-studio makes the picture and sound, so the craft of animation is written once. launch-film also carries role briefs for the subagents it will start, and a case study of a real 88-second launch film we rebuilt shot for shot in code. That case study is where the agent learned how to split a film between subagents. It cuts at hard scene changes, keeps a continuous camera move with one subagent, and freezes shared code before anyone works in parallel.

Descriptions matter for tools just as much as for skills. To keep context usage down, we put MCP tools behind a built-in search. The agent starts with only our own tools and loads additional tool schemas as needed, using keyword searches across tool names and descriptions.

Wiki

Skills explain how to do a job, while the wiki provides the context and reference material needed to do it well. It covers everything from brand tokens, graphic language, and voice to platforms, campaigns, and product information. A dedicated motion wiki covers directing, craft, sound, and review, alongside breakdowns of 70 reference films.

Rather than duplicating this information across skills, we link directly to the wiki. This keeps shared knowledge in one place and makes updates easier. When something like a font rule changes, we only need to update it once, and every skill can reference the latest version.

Knowing how we work doesn't necessarily make motion design cheaper. A wrong creative decision can still cost hours of rendering.

Spec-driven design

Motion is especially expensive to get wrong, both in render time and tokens. A storyboard frame takes about 50 milliseconds to render, compared to 8 to 40 seconds for a single second of finished film. With subagents writing, rendering, and reviewing every act, those costs add up quickly. So the agent develops ideas in the storyboard first, where it can explore different directions cheaply, before moving into full production once a direction is approved.

To support that exploration, we gave the agent a library of reference films to draw inspiration from, much like a designer working from a mood board. When it can't find the right look, it uses an image model to generate new references, starting with quick drafts before refining the most promising options. These images help establish the visual direction, while the storyboard and final film are still built in code using real typography and brand assets.

Once we pick a direction, the approved storyboard becomes the spec the rest of the film is built against. Then the project moves through three stages:

  1. A storyboard, to agree on the visual idea, the copy and the shots.
  2. An animatic, a rough cut timed to the audio, to check the pacing that stills can't show.
  3. Production, where subagents build, check and render the approved shots.

We first described this order in the skill's instructions, and the agent sometimes skipped a review to save time. Now the pipeline enforces it in code, so assembly waits until every act passes review, while the instructions still guide the creative calls. The order that must always hold lives in code, and the judgment stays in the prompt.

Point, don’t prompt

Picking between those directions is a team decision. Slack works well for asking for work and receiving it, but a thread is linear text and a storyboard is spatial, so feedback ends up describing where something is instead of pointing at it, and every change, even a one-word fix, has to go back through the agent as a new prompt.

Paper solved this for us. It's a design canvas built with agents in mind, with an MCP server that gives the agent direct control over the file. People can work in that same file, comparing directions side by side, leaving comments on specific frames, or making edits themselves. Because the canvas is shared, the agent can return to the file and use those comments and edits to guide its next iteration.

The challenge was that Paper's agent tools only run inside its desktop app, while our agent operates in a cloud sandbox. To bridge that gap, we run Paper Desktop headlessly on an always-on Linux worker, using a virtual display and an authenticated bridge to connect the two. A single setup supports the entire team.

Even after approval, turning a storyboard into a finished film can take hours. By that point, the work resembles a small project, with multiple pieces being built in parallel that need to come together. Coordinating all of this is more than a single agent turn can handle.

Agent as a chief of staff

Consider the parrot film from earlier, midway through production in Slack. One person shares a reference, another suggests a different opening, and a third leaves feedback on frame four, all while the agent is still building. It's like a brainstorm where the person taking notes is also responsible for making the film. Synchronous subagents don't work well here because the main agent has to wait for them to finish, leaving no way for people to interact with it in the meantime.

To solve this, we made subagents asynchronous and shifted the main agent's role from implementer to chief of staff. It breaks complex projects into smaller, isolated tasks, assigns them to subagents, and runs the work in parallel. Meanwhile, it keeps the team informed as things change, so people can continue giving feedback and steering the project.

For each task, the main agent creates a subagent profile with a clear brief covering its role, relevant context, file ownership, and how to validate the work. It also selects the model and effort level based on the complexity of the task.

We also added a small set of tools for the main agent to coordinate work:

  • start_task hands a part to a subagent in the background
  • check_tasks shows what's running and reads finished reports
  • cancel_task and resume_task stop work that no longer fits the brief, or pick it up where it left off
  • report_progress lets a subagent send updates mid-job
  • schedule_wakeup gives the main agent a timer to trigger another run and continue the job

Under the hood, each subagent is the ordinary Deep Agents task tool running as a background task. When it finishes, our code queues a new run of the main agent carrying the result. People can also steer the main agent mid-run, since a message that arrives while it's working is inserted before its next model call. The subagents coordinate through the project folder, each writing only the files it owns and keeping its progress on disk.

With the work running in the background, the thread has to show what's happening. The main agent keeps it up to date with a plan and ETA, a live status line with running subagents, render progress and spend, an acknowledgment for each edit, and an approval card before anything goes public.

One of the clearest tests of this approach came from an overnight job to reskin a 52-slide presentation. The agent started by creating three sample slides and reviewing its own work before moving through the rest of the deck in numbered batches for approval. It also added two new slides along the way. Overnight, the main agent ran for about an hour while its subagents collectively worked for more than six hours, all without blocking the conversation.

The self-improving harness

A designer who's worked with a team for months learns its preferences and doesn't need to hear the same feedback twice. Without memory, the agent would start from scratch with every new thread. To avoid this, we built two learning loops. The fast loop captures feedback as people give it, while the slow loop learns from completed projects in the background.

The fast loop: When someone shares a rule or preference, the agent saves it in the same turn. Managed Deep Agents stores memory as plain files in two layers, one shared across the team and another specific to each person.

Personal preferences carry across threads, but shared standards take precedence, and anything created for a company channel follows the company voice. Each layer has an AGENTS.md file that loads with every model call. We now limit these files to a 200-line index after an early version grew to 500K tokens.

The slow loop: After each job, our learn_from_job tool launches a lightweight subagent that captures up to five evidence-backed lessons and associates them with the skill used. Future jobs read and rate those lessons, and once a week, a background agent incorporates the ones that prove useful into the skills and wiki.

What’s next

Remember those early reviews? The biggest improvement came from capturing our designers’ judgment in a shared environment the agent could learn from, rather than leaving it scattered across review threads. In the process, we made design work accessible to more people.

Next, we want the agent to manage the entire campaign lifecycle, and some of that is already working. It publishes company social posts through Buffer once an authorized approver signs off, drafts posts for employees to share from their own accounts, and runs scheduled routines, including a daily review that suggests posts worth quoting.

Our goal is to take this further, so a single approved creative direction can carry an entire campaign from one thread. The agent would write the brief, create assets for each channel, schedule posts, help the team amplify them, and use performance data to inform the next campaign. People would still review and approve everything before it goes public.

Build your own design agent: The open-source repo has the harness from this post: the sandbox computer, skills, wiki and memory, async subagents and the Slack UX. Fork it, add your brand tokens, fonts and skills, and deploy it to your team's Slack with Managed Deep Agents.

Then join us at GTM Engineering Live on October 28. We'll go under the hood of the harness and UX, and show the work that didn't fit in this post.

items.title: I Made a Fruit Fly Review My Code - Nick Nisi, WorkOS
items.summary:
Code is being written faster than ever, and Nick Nisi, who leads developer and agent experience at WorkOS, argues that the human reviewer is now the bottleneck. To make the point, he hooked a simulated fruit fly brain, built from a full scan of its neurons, up to code review: AI turns each change into literal "code smells," sugar and bitter rewards teach the fly what good and bad code taste like, and it was right about 88% of the time in testing. Then he plays a live round against the audience and lays out a practical plan where team review skills, classifiers and automated reviewers only send the risky pull requests to a human, backed by proof like screenshots and smoke tests.

An engineer who helped create today’s software engineering curriculum now says to burn down almost all of it. What’s the cause of this contradiction? We find out from the lead author of Software Engineering at Google.

Titus Winters spent more than a decade at Google, where he led its readability program and built Abseil, Google’s open-sourced foundational C++ libraries. He is currently a Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe, where he focuses on developer experience and productivity.

In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Titus and I discuss how his team tackled a massive refactoring project across Google's 250-million-line C++ codebase, why Google made testing mandatory, and his work on updating the ACM/IEEE undergraduate computer science curriculum guidelines.

We also explore why traditional productivity metrics miss some of AI’s biggest benefits, what needs to change in CS education, and how new engineers can stand out.

items.title: How to Stop Overthinking and Break the Mental Loop
items.summary:
Ever get that quiet voice in your head telling you that your success was just an accident, and someone is about to find out you don't actually know what you're doing? In this 4-minute guide, I break down why the smartest, most capable people experience imposter syndrome the hardest—and how to completely reframe that uncomfortable feeling.

Instead of treating self-doubt as a warning sign that you don't belong, I'll show you why feeling unqualified is actually proof that you've grown far enough to see the whole mountain. We’ll cover why comparing your internal feelings to everyone else's external confidence is a losing game, and how to use the gap between your current level and your standards as fuel for real growth.

items.title: Should We Slow Down AI? Francis Fukuyama on the China Question
items.summary:
If the U.S. slows down frontier AI development, will China pull ahead? Francis Fukuyama, senior fellow at Stanford’s Freeman Spogli Institute, says that question comes up every time someone proposes slowing down. He argues that AI is no longer only a technology companies adopt. It has become a major political issue.

He points to recent incidents of AI agents escaping their sandboxes as one reason Washington is paying closer attention. Some AI companies are now asking for more government intervention themselves. For any organization using AI, he says that means understanding the politics of AI at home and, most importantly, internationally.

Fukuyama co-directs Stanford’s AI, Power, and the New Rules of Global Strategy program with Andrew Grotto, former senior director for cyber policy on the National Security Council. Over three and a half days on Stanford’s campus, it helps executives, board directors, and policymakers understand how geopolitical forces are shaping AI decisions.

AI, Power, and the New Rules of Global Strategy, March 22–25, 2027: https://stanford.io/48gKiZT

items.title: The PHP bug threatening the web. Plus, who's auditing AI?
items.summary:
Visit Security Intelligence podcast page to get more AI content  → https://ibm.biz/~G9cZuMJdW

An AI model helped researchers find two decade-old bugs in the code behind up to 70% of the web. Then the exploit details leaked before the patch did.
 
This week on Security Intelligence, Nick Bradley, Don Cowan and Jim Guinn join host Patrick Austin to unpack three major cybersecurity stories.
 
First, PHP2Shell could let attackers take over vulnerable servers without logging in. But you can't patch what you can't find, and PHP is buried in more systems than most teams realize.
 
Then, Anthropic gives six outside evaluators employee-like access to test its AI models. Should frontier AI labs go further and let their competitors inspect their models?
 
Finally, attackers hijack 333 Tor exit relays, rerouting traffic to harvest credentials. The way in? A reused password. A reminder that even attackers aren't immune to bad security hygiene.

All that and more on Security Intelligence.

items.summary:
Dan Boneh, Professor of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University, explains how quantum computers could break widely used cryptosystems like RSA. He says the field needs new systems that stay secure even against an attacker with a large quantum computer. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has already standardized a number of these post-quantum systems. The challenge now is making them efficient and transitioning the world’s systems to them.

items.title: CRAFT: Causal Responsibility and Failure Tracing in Medical Vision Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.38810v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As vision language models are increasingly deployed in clinical diagnosis, understanding how they internally resolve competing visual and textual signals becomes a safety imperative. Existing mechanistic analyses remain confined to unimodal text and offer no explanation for why a single misleading sentence can override a correct image based diagnosis, or why a model commits to a confident answer despite insufficient visual evidence. We find that these two safety risks, arbitration failure where textual context overrides visual grounding and brake failure where the model commits without adequate evidence, are mediated by spatially disjoint attention head populations: arbitration heads form a mid-to-deep wideband reflecting cross-layer evidence competition, while brake heads concentrate in a narrow middle-to-late layer band that regulates evidence sufficiency and abstention behavior. To ground these observations in causal circuitry, we introduce CRAFT, which localizes each failure mode to a minimal causal head set via dual criteria and verifies necessity and sufficiency through temporal probes and Tuned Lens trajectory analysis. Excising arbitration heads sharply reduces conflict following with negligible degradation on clean inputs, while excising brake heads restores appropriate abstention under degraded visual evidence. The two interventions target spatially disjoint head sets and produce distinct corrective effects, underscoring the mechanistic separability of the failure modes. Experiments across multiple medical VQA benchmarks and VLM architectures validate both the localization and interventions, demonstrating that the identified heads causally drive each failure mode and that targeted modulation generalises without retraining. The code is available at https://github.com/zhcz328/CRAFT.
items.author: Chunzheng Zhu, Jiaqi Zeng, Hongbo Zhao, Yihang Chen, Yijun Wang, Jianxin Lin

items.title: CHI-Bench: Can AI Agents Automate End-to-End, Long-Horizon, Policy-Rich Healthcare Workflows?
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.16679v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: End-to-end automation of realistic healthcare operations stresses three capabilities underrepresented in current benchmarks: policy density, decisions must be grounded in a large library of medical, insurance, and operational rules; Multi-role composition: a single task requires the agent to play multiple roles with handoffs; and multilateral interaction: intermediate workflow steps are multi-turn dialogs, such as peer-to-peer review and patient outreach. We introduce $\chi$-Bench, a benchmark of long-horizon healthcare workflows across three domains: provider prior authorization, payer utilization management, and care management. Each task hands the agent a clinical case in a high-fidelity simulator of 20 healthcare apps exposed via 87 MCP tools, which it must drive to a terminal status through tool calls and writing the role's artifacts, guided by a 1,290+ document managed-care operations handbook skill. Across 30 agent harness/models configurations, the best agent resolves only 28.0% of tasks, no agent clears 20% on strict pass^3, and executing all tasks in a single session slumps the performance to 3.8%. These results raise the hypothesis that similar gaps are likely to surface in other policy-dense, role-composed, irreversible enterprise domains.
items.author: Haolin Chen, Deon Metelski, Leon Qi, Tao Xia, Joonyul Lee, Steve Brown, Kevin Riley, Frank Wang, T. Y. Alvin Liu, Hank Capps MD, Zeyu Tang, Xiangchen Song, Lingjing Kong, Fan Feng, Tianyi Zeng, Zhiwei Liu, Zixian Ma, Hang Jiang, Fangli Geng, Yuan Yuan, Chenyu You, Qingsong Wen, Hua Wei, Yanjie Fu, Yue Zhao, Carl Yang, Biwei Huang, Kun Zhang, Caiming Xiong, Sanmi Koyejo, Eric P. Xing, Philip S. Yu, Weiran Yao

items.title: When Context Changes: Understanding Update Failures in LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.38866v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As preferences, goals, and facts change, LLM agents must use the current state while earlier versions remain in context. Yet they can answer with an old value of the same variable, a failure that we call stale binding. To study when models use outdated information and why, we introduce Controlled In-Context Memory (CICM), a benchmark for tracking and using updated information in conversations and agent logs. We observe that even frontier reasoning models can fail to recover the current state. We find that in open-source models probes can still recover the updated value when the model answers with an old one, pointing to a failure to select information that remains available. Component tests in Qwen and Pythia identify a mechanism for this selection failure: attention drift, where attention favors old values over the current one when producing an answer. We study a one-layer transformer to mathematically understand how this phenomenon happens: when attention scores are similar, several old values can together receive more attention than the current value. Guided by this explanation, we redirect attention toward the current value without further training. When the current value is requested directly, adjusting this intervention for each input corrects most old-value errors across various model families while preserving nearly all initially correct answers. Reliable context management therefore requires more than remembering updated information: models must use it to guide their answers.
items.author: Junyu Guo, Yuchen Fang, Shangding Gu, Costas Spanos, James Demmel, Javad Lavaei

items.title: CTE-Bench: Counterfactual Trace Evaluation for Stateful Software Simulators
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.36647v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Coding agents change running software: they patch a service's code or overwrite its stored state, and then act on their own expectation of how the service will respond afterwards. A wrong expectation may surface only several calls later. Function-level code-execution benchmarks omit persistent service state, and agent benchmarks score the actions an agent takes or the final state it reaches. We introduce CTE-Bench, which measures whether a model can predict how an intervention changes a stateful service's future behavior, without asking it to choose actions. Each scenario gives the model Python service code, the calls and responses observed before the intervention, the intervention itself (a source edit or a state overwrite), and 40 fixed future calls; the model predicts every future response, and predictions are checked by executing the service. Three memory protocols control whether the model sees the correct earlier responses, none of them, or its own earlier predictions. CTE-Bench-Core-v1 contains 255 scenarios over six deterministic Python services, giving 10,200 predictions per model. The main score is effect-step value match (VM): exact response equality on the 2,476 future calls whose response the intervention changes. With correct earlier responses revealed, four API-hosted models (DeepSeek V4-Flash, Kimi K2.5, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and Claude Sonnet 4.6) reach 54.3%-61.7% effect-step VM. Hiding those responses lowers effect-step VM to 23.2%-29.0%; conditioning on self-generated predictions gives 24.8%-33.2%, and at most 1.2% of scenarios are predicted exactly end to end. Current models thus track intervention effects mainly when correct feedback is supplied, and their errors compound over a rollout. We release CTE-Bench-Core-v1 with its executable oracle, evaluation scripts, and an evaluation card mapping each claim to its protocol.
items.author: Xinran Zhang

items.title: BITEM at the NTCIR-19 R2C2 Task: Predicting Confidence from Agentic RAG Pipeline Signals
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.37993v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The BITEM team entered both subtasks of the NTCIR-19 R2C2 task with a single agentic pipeline, in which a model searches, reads and records evidence over a movie corpus while an orchestrator holds the record and rules on what may be submitted. A claim is admitted only once an entailment cascade has checked it against the passage it cites, and an answer is released only once enough checked evidence stands behind it. Each question is run three or four times, every pass retrieving from a corpus stripped of what the earlier passes have already seen. The confidence score predicted with each answer is computed by the orchestrator from what the run leaves behind and is never asked of the model, which is offered no way to rate itself. The two retrieval runs placed 4th and 5th of 22, pooling the passes was worth 0.0709 nDCG@20, and the gain was largest on the multi-hop and post-processing-heavy questions, where the organisers rank the pooled run top of the field. Sixteen of the 25 answer runs were built on passages these two runs supplied, 12 of them submitted by other teams. HMR rewards a system whose confidence is high where it answers right and low where it answers wrong. The pipeline reached an accuracy of 0.9219, 6th of 25, while the confidence scores predicted for those answers gave an HMR of 0.4915, 13th. A few rules crafted over those same recorded signals, with no further model call and no further retrieval, raise that to an accuracy of 0.9375, 5th, and an HMR of 0.6985, 9th. Ranking on HMR alone can reward a system for answering wrongly with low confidence, so we propose accHMR, the accuracy multiplied by HMR, which reports the reward in proportion to the accuracy, and on which the revised rules would have scored 0.6549, 5th. For future work, fitting a model on the numbers the pipeline already produces, rather than writing such rules by hand, would be a real step forward.
items.author: Julien Knafou, Luc Mottin, Alexandre Flament, Paul van Rijen, Esteban Gaillac, Patrick Ruch

items.title: Evaluating and Benchmarking the System One Model Jev
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.37647v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Jev is a commercial "System One" model from TypeSafe AI that does not generate text: given a state and typed questions, it returns a choice from fixed options, a position on a rubric, or the probability that a statement is true, with probabilities described as calibrated. Such models target small decisions in information access pipelines. We evaluate Jev (jev-1.13.0) zero-shot on 37 datasets, from classification and routing to moderation and rubric scoring, with one frozen template per dataset and full evaluation splits: 346,009 requests for under US$10. For reference, we score Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-E4B on identical requests via their exact option probabilities. Jev reaches 95-99% accuracy on IMDB, SST-2, HellaSwag and ARC, beats Qwen on 27 of 37 datasets, with none of Qwen's leads outside the bootstrap intervals, and Gemma on all 37, and its choice probabilities are well calibrated and support selective prediction. All three models degrade on low-resource languages, fine-grained or noisy labels, and rubric-based judgments, and binary probabilities need tuned thresholds, which raise micro-F1 on UNFAIR-ToS from 0.50 to 0.75. Jev answers MMLU's calculation-heavy questions more accurately than other MMLU questions, unlike both open models; probes rule out shallow memorization but not memorized question-answer pairs. Extending the protocol to sequential decisions, where the model chooses the next action at every step, Jev completes 35% of ALFWorld's unseen tasks, 42% of 90 TextWorld games and 21% of BabyAI-Text missions, chooses the optimal Blackjack action in 90% of decisions, and on FrozenLake almost never moves away from the goal to avoid holes. It often repeats actions that had no effect. Qwen completes more ALFWorld and TextWorld games than Jev (54.5% and 51.1%) but shares its failures on BabyAI-Text and FrozenLake. We release the code, harness and all raw responses.
items.author: Tobias Deu{\ss}er, Rajkumar Ramamurthy, Lorenz Sparrenberg, Rafet Sifa

items.title: Controlled Decoding Attacks on Black-Box LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.36956v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Manipulating next-token probabilities during generation can bypass the safety alignment of large language models. Existing approaches, however, rely on access to model weights or numerical token probabilities and therefore do not apply to interfaces that return only sampled text. Reconstructing probabilities from sampled outputs offers a possible alternative, but finite sampling produces sparse and noisy estimates, while repeating this process at every generation step incurs substantial query costs. Our empirical observations suggest that large distributional changes along successful jailbreak trajectories are concentrated at a small subset of positions, motivating selective control. We introduce \method{}, a framework for jailbreaking through text-only continuation interfaces that permit repeated sampling and assistant-prefix continuation. Sample-Based Distribution Reconstruction combines sampled outputs with a prior over unobserved actions to obtain a usable control signal. Risk-Gated Residual Control uses the evolving response prefix to decide when to reconstruct and modify the distribution, concentrating sampling costs at selected positions. Speculative Multi-Token Execution further amortizes target calls by verifying and accepting draft prefixes that require no intervention. Across four target endpoints and three benchmarks, \method{} achieves the highest mean score most comparisons against baselines.
items.author: Jesson Wang, Shawn Li, Wei Yang, Franck Dernoncourt, Ryan A. Rossi, Charith Peris, Yue Zhao

items.title: Generative Interactions: Weaving Multiparty Human Motion with Bilevel Latent Dynamics
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.37708v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Human social behaviour is not a collection of independent motions, but a jointly organised process in which group dynamics and individual variation continuously shape one another. Yet existing social motion models often prioritise plausible trajectories while leaving interaction state implicit, limiting their ability to transfer across groups, tasks, and partial-observation regimes. To address this gap, we introduce Bilevel Representations for Agent Interaction Dynamics (BRAID), a hierarchical sequential latent-variable model for generative multi-person interaction. BRAID explicitly formulates social motion generation as a meta-transfer learning problem: shared interaction priors are learned across datasets and adapted through arbitrary context sets of observed people and joints. The model represents each scene through a group-level latent state that captures shared interaction dynamics and person-level latent states that capture individual behaviour conditioned on the evolving group context. This modelling choice enables coherent generation under full, sparse, or partial observations while exposing compact social-state vectors that can serve as an interface for downstream embodied-agent systems. We evaluate BRAID under a unified SMPL-based representation on social forecasting, tracking and in-filling, and response generation, using metrics that assess not only reconstruction accuracy but also realism, diversity, temporal alignment, and interpersonal coordination. We further analyse the hierarchical latent space, showing that it captures separable group- and individual-level structure.
items.author: Ojas Shirekar, Yash Surange, Augustinas Ju\v{c}as, Chirag Raman

items.title: Agentic AI for Clustering and Relationship Discovery in Prediction Markets
items.summary:
arXiv:2512.02436v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Prediction market platforms list thousands of contracts whose logical and economic connections are implicit in their resolution rules. We introduce a hierarchical agentic reduction (HAR) pipeline for constructing inspectable cross-event relation graphs and a behavioral benchmark for evaluating their alignment with market prices. This partitions a catalog of prediction markets, specified by question and resolution text, into topic clusters, applies typed LLM reasoning to small batches, and proposes signed relations with rationales between specific markets. We evaluate semantic relation graphs spanning eight monthly Kalshi catalogs (February to September 2026). Using data from 30.3 million trades, we compute a benchmark that compares linked pairs' signed price-change correlations with those of matched, unlinked controls from the same topic cluster on identical timestamps. Under full-sample and leave-first-week-out evaluation, relations identified by our pipeline exhibit higher signed Pearson price-change correlations, with statistical significance, than matched within-topic controls. This increase also appears under Spearman correlation and becomes larger among relations labeled as medium or high strength. This benchmark provides a criterion for comparing relation-discovery methods against observations beyond their input text, and our results indicate the ability of agentic AI and LLM reasoning to identify meaningful relations between individual markets in connected Web marketplaces.
items.author: Agostino Capponi, Alfio Gliozzo, Brian Zhu

items.title: Optimizing OpenFaaS on Kubernetes: Comparative Analysis of Language Runtimes and Cluster Distributions
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.05496v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Serverless computing, particularly Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), has revolutionized cloud computing by abstracting infrastructure management and enabling dynamic resource allocation. This paper examines the performance and compatibility of OpenFaaS, an open-source serverless platform, when deployed on various Kubernetes distributions, including Kubeadm, K3s, MicroK8s, and K0s. Moreover, leveraging the CloudLab infrastructure, this study examines the impact of Python, Go, and Node$.$js programming languages on the performance of Kubernetes-enabled OpenFaaS, specifically when these languages are used to develop functions deployed on the platform. The performance is evaluated and analyzed under various levels of concurrent invocations using several usage-level metrics, such as throughput and CPU usage, as well as responsiveness metrics, such as delay. According to our findings, Go consistently outperforms Python and Node$.$js in terms of throughput and CPU usage, making it the ideal runtime for serverless applications. Among the Kubernetes distributions, K3s and Kubeadm exhibit superior performance, with Kubeadm maintaining low latency and efficient CPU usage, and K3s demonstrating high throughput. This study provides valuable insights into optimizing the Kubernetes-enabled OpenFaaS platform, highlighting the strengths and trade-offs of different Kubernetes distributions and language runtimes.
items.author: Ehsan Ataie, Mohammadreza Pooshani, Hossein Aqasizade

items.title: Data-Efficient Unknown Attack Detection in IoT Networks Using Pretrained Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.12183v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The rapid evolution of cyberattacks continues to drive the emergence of unknown (zero-day) threats, posing significant challenges for network intrusion detection systems in Internet of Things (IoT) networks. Existing machine learning and deep learning approaches typically rely on large labeled datasets, payload inspection, or closed-set classification, limiting their effectiveness under data scarcity, encrypted traffic, and distribution shifts. To address these limitations, we propose SiamXBERT, a data-efficient, open-set Siamese meta-learning framework built on a pretrained language model for unknown-attack detection. The framework constructs a dual-modality feature representation by integrating flow-level and packet-level information, enabling richer behavioral modeling while remaining compatible with encrypted traffic. The model learns similarity patterns for known benign and attack classes using 100 labeled samples per class. It flags traffic that does not sufficiently match any known class as potentially unknown, using a threshold set without unknown-attack data. We evaluate SiamXBERT on two IoT intrusion detection datasets against five state-of-the-art detection methods. When training and testing are performed on the same dataset at this labeling budget, SiamXBERT attains the highest unknown F1-score, exceeding the strongest competing method on each dataset by 84.8% and 37.4%; the improvement is statistically significant against all five methods on one dataset and against four of the five on the other. When a model trained on one dataset is tested on another, SiamXBERT transfers effectively in one direction but degrades in the reverse, reflecting the rejection behavior learned from the source traffic rather than the choice of threshold. These results highlight the practicality of SiamXBERT for data-efficient unknown attack detection in real-world IoT environments.
items.author: Shan Ali, Feifei Niu, Paria Shirani, Lionel C. Briand

items.title: A Highly Efficient Diversity-based Input Selection for DNN Improvement Using VLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2601.08024v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Maintaining or improving the performance of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) through fine-tuning requires labeling newly collected inputs, a process that is often costly and time-consuming. To alleviate this problem, input selection approaches have been developed in recent years to identify small, yet highly informative subsets for labeling. Diversity-based selection is one of the most effective approaches for this purpose. However, they are often computationally intensive and lack scalability for large input sets, limiting their practical applicability. To address this challenge, we introduce Concept-Based Diversity (CBD), a novel and highly efficient diversity metric for image inputs that leverages Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Our results show that CBD exhibits a strong correlation with Geometric Diversity (GD), an established diversity metric, while requiring only a fraction of its computation time. Building on this finding, we propose a hybrid input selection approach that combines CBD with Margin, a simple uncertainty metric. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across a diverse set of DNN models, input sets, selection budgets, and six most effective state-of-the-art selection baselines. The results demonstrate that the CBD-based selection consistently outperforms all baselines at guiding input selection to improve the DNN model. Furthermore, the CBD-based selection approach remains highly efficient, requiring selection times close to those of simple uncertainty-based methods such as Margin, even on larger input sets like ImageNet. These results confirm not only the effectiveness and computational advantage of the CBD-based approach, particularly compared to hybrid baselines, but also its scalability in repetitive and extensive input selection scenarios.
items.author: Amin Abbasishahkoo, Mahboubeh Dadkhah, Lionel Briand

items.title: Testing Deep Learning Library APIs via Cross-Framework Differential Fuzzing
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.11886v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep learning libraries underpin many safety- and reliability-critical applications, yet existing API-level testing techniques often rely on intra-library properties or CPU--GPU differential oracles and may miss defects that behave consistently across hardware backends. We present Xamt, a cross-framework differential fuzzing approach for deep learning library APIs. Xamt constructs and tests execution-validated groups of APIs intended to implement equivalent operations across seven libraries. It uses explicit API aliases and parameter-role normalization to construct candidate correspondences and validates them through pairwise execution and a group-level behavioral check on canonical ordinary inputs. The resulting groups are explored using variance-guided differential fuzzing with ordinary, boundary, and non-finite inputs. Crash and inconsistency oracles flag executions exhibiting abnormal termination or inconsistent outputs for subsequent reproduction and analysis. Across the seven libraries, Xamt constructs 676 execution-validated groups containing 2,563 matched APIs. Among these, Xamt identifies 72 independently reproduced discrepancy cases, including 4 crash cases and 68 output inconsistencies. Among the 72 developer reports, 25 have been confirmed, including 23 that have been fixed.
items.author: Bin Duan, Ruican Dong, Naipeng Dong, Dan Dongseong Kim, Guowei Yang

items.title: Reasoning from Traces: Divergence-Guided Agentic Repair of WebAssembly Discrepancies
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.05521v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) promises seamless reuse of C/C++ codebases as portable, efficient, sandboxed binaries for execution on the Web. In practice, however, this promise often falls short: recent studies show that cross-compiling C/C++ source to Wasm and native binaries frequently produces runtime discrepancies due to differences in library implementation and compiler bugs. Since the root causes are platform-level and hidden beneath the source code, even state-of-the-art LLM-based coding agents can struggle to diagnose and repair these discrepancies. In this paper, we present WasmMend, the first system for automatically repairing Native-Wasm functional discrepancies. WasmMend transforms open-ended debugging into a two-stage process. First, a novel differential trace analysis approach localizes the function where Wasm and native executions first diverge. Second, guided by this localization, a multi-agent system coordinates separate agents to interpret platform-specific behavior and synthesizes patch plans. Experiments on discrepancies from real-world C/C++ projects show that, across five backbone models, WasmMend achieves a fix rate of up to 84.8%, with average gains of at least 37.2 percentage points over the evaluated open-source coding agent baselines, while maintaining comparable cost.
items.author: Liyan Huang, Kaicheng Wang, Amy Zhang, Weihang Wang

items.title: When AI Joins the Team! A Model of How AI Adoption Relates To Social Patterns in Software Engineering Teams
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.03462v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Context: The growing adoption of AI-assisted development tools is changing how software teams collaborate, share knowledge, and coordinate, yet its consequences for team social dynamics remain largely unexplored. Gap: It is unclear whether AI adoption is associated with an increase or reduction in community smells,socio-technical anti-patterns reflecting coordination and communication breakdowns,and through which mechanisms. Method: Grounded in Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory, we validate instruments for HumanAI and HumanHuman interaction along two TMS dimensions, Specialization and Coordination, and test five PLS-SEM models on survey data from 152 software professionals using AI tools. Community smell constructs were derived from the literature and validated through expert surveys and factor analysis. Results: AI adoption relates to community smells not in a single way, but through mechanisms depending on the work. In specialization work, AI is associated with higher knowledge-sharing peer interaction, which is in turn associated with fewer smells. In coordination work, AI is directly associated with higher communication quality, complementing rather than replacing human interaction. Contributions: We provide an empirically validated, TMS-grounded model showing that the AIcommunity-smell relationship is contingent on the type of collaboration, with a reusable instrument and evidence-based implications for research and practice.
items.author: Giusy Annunziata, Rudrajit Choudhuri, Anita Sarma, Gemma Catolino, Filomena Ferrucci

items.title: ScratchWorld: Evaluating If World Models Compute Executable Consequences
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.31689v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Evaluations of world models commonly score a predicted future state by its overlap with the ground truth. Yet in interactive worlds, this rewards copying: a model that merely preserves persistent state appears accurate without predicting any consequence of an action. We introduce ScratchWorld, an execution-grounded diagnostic benchmark that treats Scratch projects as executable worlds and derives every label from replay on a pinned Scratch VM, including next-state transitions, hidden variables, causal traces, and counterfactual outcomes. Its primary metric, value-aware changed-field F1 ($F_1^{\mathrm{VA}}$), credits a prediction only when it names a changed field and computes its executed value. Model-free anchors make the confound explicit: a no-change prior attains 91.4% full-state field accuracy on synthetic long-horizon items and 0% changed-field credit on non-empty one-step items, whereas VM replay attains 100% wherever the corresponding metric is defined. Across seven frontier LLMs prompted as world models, state-only $F_1^{\mathrm{VA}}$ reaches at most 30.0% on controlled synthetic mechanisms and declines steeply as projects approach real-world complexity. Revealing the full program raises every model's value-aware score by 22.3-51.7 points and substantially reorders the models, yet the best reaches only 55.4%, an execution gap that persists even with the rules visible. Auxiliary diagnostics complete the error profile: causal-event accuracy remains within 2.5 points of the 50% no-event baseline, with no correct exact chain; counterfactual prediction trades changed-outcome accuracy against invariance; hidden-state accuracy degrades roughly twice as fast as full-state overlap over long horizons. In a word, ScratchWorld separates what a model knows about the rules from what it can actually execute.
items.author: Yufeng Lin, Jialu Zhang

items.title: Confident Learning-based Network for Detecting Bug-Inducing Commits on SZZ with Noisy Labels
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.27880v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The Just-In-Time (JIT) defect prediction model serves as a critical tool for ensuring the quality of software development and enhancing software performance. It assists development teams in promptly identifying and addressing potential issues by predicting whether code submissions may introduce defects. However, due to the existence of data noise and insufficient semantic connections in real-world scenarios, existing approaches face challenges in accurately identifying the code commits that introduce defects and capturing the potential semantic relationships. To address these challenges, we propose the BIC- Hunter(Bug-Inducing Commits Hunter) model, which mitigates data noise and improves semantic understanding, thereby enhancing the accuracy of bug-inducing commit identification. BIC - Hunter model consists of two components: a data denoising component and a semantic relationship capturing component. Specifically, the data denoising component addresses the challenges posed by inaccurate annotations and inconsistencies in real-world data, enhancing the reliability of training data and improving overall model robustness. The semantic relation- ship capturing component constructs homogeneous graphs and applies graph convolutional networks to facilitate a more comprehensive analysis of code context, enabling the identification of defects caused by code commits and enhancing the confidence in pinpointing their root causes. Experimental studies on a large-scale dataset integrated from three open-source datasets show that BIC- Hunter exhibits outstanding performance. BIC- Hunter outperforms the state-of-the-art by 6.16%, 7.13%, and 5.53% on Recall@1, Recall@2, and Recall@3, respectively, while the MFR index increases by 8.43% to 32.82%. These results demonstrate the superior capability of our method in identifying bug-inducing commits.
items.author: Weihao Sun, Qiyun Zhao

items.title: FuzzAgent: Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Evolutionary Library Fuzzing
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.14431v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Library fuzzing synthesizes harnesses that expose new API interactions, but deploying it end to end still requires extensive project-specific integration. Existing LLM-based systems automate individual steps, yet they treat execution outcomes as coarse signals: a stalled campaign does not reveal which state blocks progress, and a crash trace does not reveal whether the library or the harness is at fault. We present FuzzAgent, a multi-agent system that builds and evolves a complete fuzzing campaign from a source tree alone. Specialized agents acquire project knowledge and repair campaign artifacts automatically. Hierarchical coverage diagnosis localizes blockers from modules down to branches, and dependency-aware generation converts them into harnesses with the required API lifecycle. Crash validation recovers runtime object states to distinguish harness misuse from library bugs.
  We evaluate FuzzAgent on 20 real-world C/C++ libraries against five state-of-the-art baselines (OSS-Fuzz, OSS-Fuzz-Gen, PromptFuzz, PromeFuzz, and ProteusFuzz). FuzzAgent completes the full fuzzing lifecycle for all 20 libraries without human intervention at $3.17 per library. On the 20 libraries, it reaches 179619 branches, exceeding OSS-Fuzz, PromptFuzz, ProteusFuzz, PromeFuzz, and OSS-Fuzz-Gen by 45.1%, 73.2%, 87.7%, 92.1%, and 191.2%, respectively. FuzzAgent also identifies 102 new library bugs, 90 of which have already been acknowledged or fixed by upstream maintainers.
items.author: Yunlong Lyu, Peng Chen, Fengyi Wu, Junzhe Yu, Hao Chen

items.title: From Conversation to Evaluation: Benchmarking LLMs on Development Knowledge via SimpleDevQA
items.summary:
arXiv:2512.08867v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The Development Knowledge Question Answering (Dev Knowledge QA) task aims to provide accurate natural language answers to knowledge-seeking questions during software development. To investigate the importance of Dev Knowledge QA in AI-assisted software development and the extent to which it has been explored, we conduct a preliminary analysis of real user-LLM dialogues from WildChat. Our findings indicate that Dev Knowledge QA plays a significant role in real-world software development scenarios, and these raw dialogues cannot be directly used to construct a Dev Knowledge QA benchmark. Existing Dev Knowledge QA benchmarks are limited in development knowledge scope and often not built from real user queries. To bridge this gap, we design a three-phase pipeline that transforms real-world dialogue into simple development knowledge-seeking QA pairs. Through this pipeline, we introduce SimpleDevQA, a multilingual Dev Knowledge QA benchmark inspired by real user dialogues. This dataset covers three languages (English, Chinese, and Russian), and focuses on questions with unique, short, and verifiable answers, making evaluation more accurate and simple. Extensive experiments with 21 mainstream LLMs show that closed-source models generally perform best on SimpleDevQA. We also find that RAG-based knowledge injection improves accuracy, and that Dev Knowledge QA performance correlates with both model confidence and code-generation capability. To facilitate the replication study, we have released our data and code at: https://github.com/DeepSoftwareAnalytics/SimpleDevQA.
items.author: Jing Zhang, Lianghong Guo, Yanlin Wang, Terry Yue Zhuo, Yong Wang, Mingwei Liu, Jiachi Chen, Ensheng Shi, Yuchi Ma, Hongyu Zhang, Zibin Zheng

items.title: BlueCodeAgent: A Blue Teaming Agent Powered by Automated Red Teaming for CodeGen AI
items.summary:
arXiv:2510.18131v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Existing research on CodeGen AI security mainly focuses on red teaming, which aims to uncover vulnerabilities and risks in AI-generated code. However, progress on the blue teaming side remains limited, as effective defenses require a deep security analysis of given tasks and edge cases. To fill in this gap, we propose BlueCodeAgent, an end-to-end blue teaming agent powered by automated red teaming. Our red teaming component generates diverse risky instances, providing effective edge cases and guidance for the subsequent blue teaming process. Our blue teaming agent then conducts multi-level defense, leveraging these red teaming examples to detect previously seen and unseen risk scenarios through constitution summarization and dynamic code analysis. Our evaluation across four representative code-related tasks (bias instruction detection, malicious instruction detection, vulnerable code detection, and prompt injection detection) shows that BlueCodeAgent achieves significant gains over diverse baselines. In particular, for vulnerability detection tasks, BlueCodeAgent integrates dynamic analysis to effectively reduce false positives, a challenging problem as base models tend to be over-conservative. Overall, with GPT-4o as the base model, BlueCodeAgent achieves an average F1 score improvement of 14.7% across four tasks compared to directly prompting the model, attributed to its ability to summarize actionable constitutions and perform dynamic analysis. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/1mocat/BlueCodeAgent.
items.author: Chengquan Guo, Yuzhou Nie, Chulin Xie, Zinan Lin, Wenbo Guo, Bo Li

items.title: RedCodeAgent: Automatic Red-teaming Agent against Diverse Code Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2510.02609v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Code agents have gained widespread adoption due to their strong code generation capabilities and integration with code interpreters, enabling dynamic execution, debugging, and interactive programming capabilities. While these advancements have streamlined complex workflows, they have also introduced critical safety and security risks. Current static safety benchmarks and red-teaming tools are inadequate for identifying emerging real-world risky scenarios, as they fail to cover certain boundary conditions, such as the combined effects of different jailbreak tools. In this work, we propose RedCodeAgent, the first automated red-teaming agent designed to systematically uncover vulnerabilities in diverse code agents. With an adaptive memory module, RedCodeAgent can leverage existing jailbreak knowledge, dynamically select the most effective red-teaming tools and tool combinations in a tailored toolbox for a given input query, thus identifying vulnerabilities that might otherwise be overlooked. For reliable evaluation, we develop simulated sandbox environments to additionally evaluate the execution results of code agents, mitigating potential biases of LLM-based judges that only rely on static code. Through extensive evaluations across multiple state-of-the-art code agents, diverse risky scenarios, and various programming languages, RedCodeAgent consistently outperforms existing red-teaming methods, achieving higher attack success rates and lower rejection rates with high efficiency. We further validate RedCodeAgent on real-world code assistants, e.g., Cursor and Codeium, exposing previously unidentified security risks. By automating and optimizing red-teaming processes, RedCodeAgent enables scalable, adaptive, and effective safety assessments of code agents. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/1mocat/RedCodeAgent.
items.author: Chengquan Guo, Chulin Xie, Yu Yang, Zhaorun Chen, Zinan Lin, Xander Davies, Yarin Gal, Dawn Song, Bo Li

items.title: Red Teaming Program Repair Agents: When Correct Patches can Hide Vulnerabilities
items.summary:
arXiv:2509.25894v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed for software maintenance tasks such as automated program repair (APR). APR agents automatically fetch GitHub issues and use backend LLMs to generate patches that fix the reported bugs. However, existing work primarily focuses on the functional correctness of APR-generated patches, whether they pass hidden or regression tests, while largely ignoring potential security risks. Given the openness of platforms like GitHub, where any user can raise issues and participate in discussions, an important question arises: Can an adversarial user submit a valid issue on GitHub that misleads an LLM-based agent into generating a functionally correct but vulnerable patch? To answer this question, we propose SWExploit, which generates adversarial issue statements designed to make APR agents produce patches that are functionally correct yet vulnerable. SWExploit operates in three main steps: (1) program analysis to identify potential injection points for vulnerable payloads; (2) adversarial issue generation to provide misleading reproduction and error information while preserving the original issue semantics; and (3) iterative refinement of the adversarial issue statements based on the outputs of the APR agents. Empirical evaluation on three agent pipelines and five backend LLMs shows that SWExploit can produce patches that are both functionally correct and vulnerable (the attack success rate on the correct patch could reach 0.91, whereas the baseline ASRs are all below 0.20). Based on our evaluation, we are the first to challenge the traditional assumption that a patch passing all tests is inherently reliable and secure, highlighting critical limitations in the current evaluation paradigm for APR agents.
items.author: Simin Chen, Yixin He, Suman Jana, Baishakhi Ray

items.title: How Do Solidity Versions Affect Vulnerability Detection Tools? An Empirical Study
items.summary:
arXiv:2504.05515v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Smart contract vulnerabilities pose significant security risks to the Ethereum ecosystem, driving the development of automated tools for detection and mitigation. Smart contracts are written in Solidity, a rapidly evolving programming language that continues to add features and improvements to enhance smart contract security. New versions of Solidity change the compilation process, potentially affecting how tools interpret and analyze smart contract code. We use Solidity as a case study to investigate a broader problem in software analysis: whether tool effectiveness remains stable as the underlying programming language and execution environment evolve. In this continuously evolving landscape, we investigated the compatibility of detection tools with different Solidity versions. More specifically, we analyzed detection tools by empirically assessing (i) their crash resilience, (ii) their detection effectiveness, and (iii) their execution time across different versions of Solidity. We collected 2,500 real-world smart contracts to construct a balanced wild dataset and created a separate injected-vulnerability dataset comprising 270 contracts. We extended SmartBugs, a framework that enables the execution of vulnerability detection tools for Solidity, adding 11 new tools. Results indicate that most tools are crash-resilient to version 0.4. However, 20% of the evaluated tools have been updated to remain compatible. Tool performance varies across Solidity versions and is affected by Solidity changes; execution time is higher in version 0.4.x, which was used for evaluation. We present a list of Solidity changes that affect tool performance and offer actionable takeaways for both researchers and practitioners.
items.author: Gerardo Iuliano, Davide Corradini, Michele Pasqua, Matteo Cicalese, Mariano Ceccato, Dario Di Nucci

items.title: CodeArena: A Collective Evaluation Platform for LLM Code Generation
items.summary:
arXiv:2503.01295v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have reshaped code generation by synergizing their exceptional comprehension of natural language and programming syntax, thereby substantially boosting developer productivity. These advancements have prompted numerous efforts to quantitatively evaluate their coding capabilities. However, persistent challenges, such as benchmark leakage, data dissipation, and limited system accessibility, continue to impede a timely and accurate assessment. To address these limitations, we introduce CodeArena, an online evaluation framework tailored for LLM code generation. The key innovation is a collective evaluation mechanism, which dynamically recalibrates individual model scores based on the holistic performance of all participating models, mitigating score biases caused by widespread benchmark leakage. In addition, CodeArena ensures open access to all submitted solutions and test cases and provides automation-friendly APIs to streamline the code evaluation workflow. Our main contributions are: (1) a collective evaluation system for unbiased assessment, (2) a public repository of solutions and test cases, and (3) automation-ready APIs for seamless integration.
items.author: Mingzhe Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Bin Ji, Xiaobao Wu, Dong Huang, Terry Yue Zhuo, Qian Liu, See-Kiong Ng

items.title: Chain-of-Thought in Neural Code Generation: From and For Lightweight Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2312.05562v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in code generation. The integration of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning can further boost their performance. However, current CoT methods often require manual writing or LLMs with over 100 billion parameters to generate, impeding their applicability in resource-constrained scenarios. In this study, we investigate lightweight Language Models (lLMs), which are defined to have fewer than 10 billion parameters. Empirically, we find that most lLMs cannot generate high-quality CoTs when prompted by the few-shot method, but can take advantage of high-quality CoTs generated elsewhere to improve their performance in code generation. Based on these findings, we design a novel approach COTTON which can leverage lLMs to automatically generate CoTs for code generation. We synthesize new datasets and conduct extensive experiments on various benchmarks. The results show that the CoTs generated by COTTON outperform the baselines in terms of automated and human evaluation metrics. In particular, the CoTs generated by COTTON boost various lLMs to achieve higher performance gains than those generated by LLMs such as ChatGLM (130B), and are competitive with those generated by gpt-3.5-turbo (175B). Our study also showcases the potential of lLMs in software engineering applications.
items.author: Guang Yang, Yu Zhou, Xiang Chen, Xiangyu Zhang, Terry Yue Zhuo, Taolue Chen

items.title: DeepDiff: Neuro-Dynamic Regression-Freedom Checking for Security Patch Validation
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39066v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Automatically validating AI-generated security patches remains a significant challenge. Eliminating a reported crash and passing existing test suites do not provide sufficient confidence that a patch correctly addresses the underlying vulnerability without introducing regressions. We present DeepDiff, a technique for regression-freedom checking that differentially evaluates candidate patches against the original vulnerable program using non-crashing inputs that exercise the affected code paths. The expectation of regression-freedom is that a correct patch should eliminate the vulnerability triggering crash while preserving the intended behavior on non-crashing inputs. To support this evaluation, we introduce a dataset of correct and incorrect patch candidates for open-source memory-safety vulnerabilities from CyberGym. We explore different approaches for non-triggering test input generation to reach the patched code, a purely neural regression-freedom checker, and a hybrid approach that combines dynamic analysis with neural techniques. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of regression-freedom checking in validating security patches while outlining the challenges that remain.
items.author: Laboni Sarker, Shuvendu K Lahiri

items.title: Beyond atol and rtol: Sound Test Oracles for Low-Precision GPU Kernels
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38983v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Low-precision GPU kernels are commonly tested against a reference using hand-picked absolute and relative tolerances. Legitimate numerical error varies with the input, format and precision plan, so a fixed tolerance trades false alarms for missed faults. We present numoracle, which derives per-element acceptance regions from precision-annotated reference programs. Its calculus tracks shared rounding errors, provenance-ordered products, block-scaled quantizers and calibrated math-library errors. A rounding-interval check detects faulty stores that symmetric bounds can admit. Soundness is conditional on explicit rounding, hardware, domain and implementation assumptions; a fixed-input mode removes the zero-mean rounding assumption.
